subChunks.title: Circuit Breaker, Retry, Bulkhead & Timeout
subChunks.hookHtml: Distributed systems fail partially — a downstream service may be slow, intermittently unavailable, or completely down. Without resilience patterns, these partial failures cascade into full system outages. Circuit breakers, retries, bulkheads, and timeouts are the patterns that keep your service alive when the world around it is broken.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Retry Pattern

Transient failures (network blips, momentary unavailability) often resolve on their own. Retry with exponential backoff gives the downstream service time to recover.

// Retry with exponential backoff
int maxAttempts = 3;
long delayMs = 100;
for (int attempt = 1; attempt <= maxAttempts; attempt++) {
    try {
        return callDownstream();
    } catch (TransientException e) {
        if (attempt == maxAttempts) throw e;
        Thread.sleep(delayMs * (1L << (attempt - 1))); // 100ms, 200ms, 400ms
    }
}

Add jitter to the backoff (random variation) to prevent thundering-herd: all callers retrying at the same time amplifies the load on the recovering service.

Circuit Breaker Pattern

Inspired by electrical circuit breakers. Three states:

  • CLOSED: normal operation; requests pass through; failures counted
  • OPEN: too many failures; requests fail immediately without calling downstream (fail fast); prevents load on a failing service
  • HALF-OPEN: after a timeout, one probe request is allowed; if it succeeds, circuit closes; if it fails, circuit stays open

Key parameters: failure threshold (e.g. 5 failures in 10 seconds), open duration (e.g. 30 seconds before half-open), success threshold for re-closing.

Bulkhead Pattern

Isolate failure domains by limiting concurrent calls per dependency. Named after the watertight compartments in a ship — flooding one compartment does not flood all. In Java: use separate thread pools or semaphores per external dependency.

// Semaphore-based bulkhead: max 10 concurrent calls to payment service
Semaphore paymentBulkhead = new Semaphore(10);

public PaymentResult charge(Payment p) throws Exception {
    if (!paymentBulkhead.tryAcquire(500, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) {
        throw new BulkheadFullException("Payment service bulkhead full");
    }
    try {
        return paymentClient.charge(p);
    } finally {
        paymentBulkhead.release();
    }
}

Timeout Pattern

Every network call must have a timeout. A service that never times out will block threads indefinitely, exhausting the thread pool. Set connect timeout (time to establish connection) and read timeout (time to receive response) separately.

Timeout values: too aggressive causes spurious failures; too lenient allows slow services to exhaust resources. Start with p99 latency + buffer, then tune from observability data.

Combining Patterns

In production these patterns compose: Timeout (don't wait forever) → Retry (try again on transient failure) → CircuitBreaker (stop retrying a broken service) → Bulkhead (limit blast radius per dependency). Libraries: Resilience4j (Java), Spring Cloud Circuit Breaker.

storyBeats.text: The Academy's spell enrichment service called three downstream services on every spell cast. One night the rune-lookup service went slow — response times climbed to 30 seconds. Every spell-cast thread blocked waiting. In 90 seconds the entire spell execution thread pool was exhausted. The Academy stopped responding to all requests — not because of the bad service, but because there was no circuit breaker.

storyBeats.speaker: Reliability Engineer Saar
storyBeats.text: Cascade failure is how simple partial failures become full outages. One slow dependency holds your threads. Your threads fill up. You stop responding. Your callers time out and retry — amplifying the load. Everything falls down. The circuit breaker exists to break this chain: fail fast when the downstream is broken, let it recover, then try again.

storyBeats.speaker: Reliability Engineer Saar
storyBeats.text: A retry without a circuit breaker is dangerous. If the downstream is fully down, every retry adds load to an already struggling service — exactly when it needs relief. The circuit breaker opens and stops retries for a period. The downstream gets breathing room to recover. Then the half-open probe tests recovery. This is engineered compassion for your dependencies.

storyBeats.speaker: Circuit breaker state machine
Reliability Engineer Saar
storyBeats.text: The bulkhead is the resilience pattern most often forgotten. Without it, a slow payment service can consume all your threads — even though inventory and shipping are fine. Bulkheads ensure that each dependency gets a limited resource quota. A flooded payment bulkhead only affects payment calls. Everything else continues working.

learningObjectives: Describe the three states of a circuit breaker and the transitions between them
Implement exponential backoff with jitter for retry logic
Explain how the bulkhead pattern limits blast radius using semaphores or thread pool isolation
Compose multiple resilience patterns (timeout → retry → circuit breaker → bulkhead) and explain the order
commonMistakes: Retrying without a circuit breaker — amplifies load on a failing dependency
Using the same thread pool for all external dependencies — a slow dependency exhausts threads for all callers
Setting timeouts too aggressively without understanding p99 latency — causes spurious failures
Not adding jitter to retry backoff — thundering herd can overload a recovering service
assessmentCriteria: Can draw the circuit breaker state machine (CLOSED/OPEN/HALF-OPEN) with correct transitions
Can implement a retry with exponential backoff in Java from scratch
Can explain why a bulkhead prevents one slow dependency from affecting the whole application
Can describe the correct order for composing timeout, retry, circuit breaker, and bulkhead
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a developer why their service can go down even though the failing component is someone else's service. Walk through the cascade failure scenario and explain which resilience pattern prevents each step of the cascade.
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Implement a simple CircuitBreaker class with three states (CLOSED, OPEN, HALF_OPEN):

  1. Fields: State state (enum), int failureCount, int failureThreshold (e.g. 3), long openedAt, long openDurationMs (e.g. 2000)
  2. Method void recordFailure() — increments failureCount; opens circuit if threshold reached (store openedAt)
  3. Method void recordSuccess() — resets failureCount, sets state to CLOSED
  4. Method boolean allowRequest() — CLOSED: always true; OPEN: check if openDuration elapsed → if yes, move to HALF_OPEN and return true; if no, return false; HALF_OPEN: return true
  5. In main: simulate 3 failures → verify OPEN → sleep 2.1s → verify request allowed (HALF_OPEN) → simulate success → verify CLOSED
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
Write a class RetryWithBackoff that wraps a Callable<String> with retry logic:

  • Method String execute(Callable<String> task, int maxAttempts)
  • Exponential backoff: 100ms, 200ms, 400ms (2^(attempt-1) * 100ms), capped at 400ms
  • Add random jitter of 0–50ms to each delay
  • On final failure, throw the last exception wrapped in a RuntimeException
  • In main: create a counter starting at 0; pass a Callable that throws RuntimeException for the first 2 calls and returns 'success' on the third. Verify it returns 'success' after 2 retries. Also test a Callable that always fails — confirm RuntimeException is thrown.

soloPracticeTests.label: RuntimeException thrown after all attempts fail

questions.prompt: A circuit breaker is in the OPEN state. What happens when a new request arrives?
options: The request is queued for later processing
The request is forwarded to a backup service
The request fails immediately without calling the downstream service
The circuit enters HALF-OPEN state and the request is forwarded
questions.answer: The request fails immediately without calling the downstream service
questions.explanation: When the circuit is OPEN, requests fail immediately (fail fast) without touching the downstream service. This prevents your threads from blocking on a known-broken dependency and gives the downstream service time to recover. The circuit remains OPEN for a configured duration, then enters HALF-OPEN to test recovery with one probe request.

questions.prompt: Why should retry logic include jitter (random variation) in the backoff delay?
options: To make the code less predictable and harder to exploit
To prevent all retrying clients from hitting the downstream service simultaneously after a failure
To compensate for clock skew across distributed nodes
Java requires randomness to avoid deterministic failures
questions.answer: To prevent all retrying clients from hitting the downstream service simultaneously after a failure
questions.explanation: Without jitter, all clients that failed at the same time will retry at the same time (e.g. all at T+100ms). This thundering herd can overwhelm a recovering service with a sudden spike. Jitter spreads retries across a time window, distributing the load and giving the recovering service a better chance to stabilise.

questions.prompt: Your service calls three downstream APIs: payment, inventory, and shipping. The payment service becomes slow (20s responses). Without a bulkhead, what happens to inventory and shipping calls?
options: Nothing — they use separate HTTP clients
They are unaffected — Java handles I/O asynchronously by default
Threads waiting for payment fill up the shared thread pool, blocking inventory and shipping calls too
The JVM automatically isolates failures between different HTTP clients
questions.answer: Threads waiting for payment fill up the shared thread pool, blocking inventory and shipping calls too
questions.explanation: If all three clients share a common thread pool (e.g. the HTTP server's request thread pool), slow payment calls will hold threads for 20 seconds each. As the pool fills up, new requests — even those only needing inventory or shipping — cannot get a thread. This is cascade failure from a single slow dependency. A bulkhead (separate pool or semaphore per client) limits how many threads can block on payment, preserving capacity for other calls.
